answers.justification: C1 shows early-action yield fell by the same amount (45.2→37.8%, −7.4 pts) as regular-decision yield (39.0→31.5%, −7.5 pts), even though EA decisions went out on time on the legacy system (E2). Turnaround therefore does not explain the yield fall.

C2 shows yield fell about 13 points only in the tiers whose awards were cut (Dean's 45.2→31.9%, Merit 44.9→32.3%). Yield was flat for Presidential (unchanged award) and no-merit admits, tier criteria were the same in both years, competitors made no merit changes (C8), and cost reasons rose in the survey (C3).
Applications rose (9,850→10,240), admits rose (5,120→5,270) and admitted GPA rose (3.61→3.63) (E2). Regional graduate numbers were broadly flat for 2026 (C7).

51 of the 64 'missing document' tickets were closed as present after a status refresh, which points to display lag (C4, C5, E4). But 13 were auto-closed with no resolution note, and the log has no file contents or completion times, so actual loss of documents is unlikely but not ruled out.
C2 shows the drop was not shared by all groups: Presidential yield held at 36.6→36.2% and no-merit yield at 38.5→37.0%, while the tiers with cut awards fell about 13 points.
The EA versus RD comparison in C1 shows equal yield drops whether or not decisions were slowed, which counts against turnaround causing the fall.

C2 works like a natural experiment: the tiers with cut awards lost about 13 points of yield, unchanged tiers held steady, criteria did not change, and the drop appears in both EA and RD (C1). The mechanism is shown by more cost-related reasons (C3) and more appeals (C14).

The reader freeze coincided with the backlog and slower merit-file turnaround (C6, C1), but the scoring-module outage happened at the same time. The records cannot separate the two, and there is no four-reader legacy comparison (C6, E4).
The applicant pool was larger and slightly stronger (E2), so a smaller or weaker pool cannot explain the enrolment fall.
The yield loss traces to the finance committee's award schedule (E5, C2), not to Admissions performance (C1). Replacing the director would punish the wrong party and leave the cause in place.

A2 targets the evidenced cause in the specific tiers that lost yield (C2), and it is timed before the next award letters. Modelling the revenue trade-off is needed because total first-year net tuition fell 10.4% even though net tuition per student rose (C15).

RD delays were real and annoyed counsellors (E2, E3, C3), so a turnaround target is reasonable. However, it does not address the yield fall (C1), and the bottleneck lies in staffing and the scoring module (C6), which Admissions does not fully control.
Most document-status tickets were display lag that cleared on refresh (C4, C5), so document loss (H4) is unconfirmed and a full module rebuild is not yet justified.

The tier-level and round-level comparisons (C2, C1), backed by the survey (C3), stable competitor pricing (C8) and the revenue report (C15), give enough evidence to commit to taking a modelled restoration proposal to the finance committee.

ambiguousItems: S04: H4 could reasonably be 'contradicted' (51 of 64 tickets were status lag, and the vendor and director both say files were complete) or 'unknown' (13 tickets were auto-closed with no resolution and there are no file-completion data).
S12: A3 could be 'acceptable' or 'premature', because the turnaround bottleneck (staffing vs module) is unresolved and Admissions may not control it.
S13: A4 could be 'premature' or 'harmful', since rebuilding a module that seems to work wastes resources before the next cycle.
caseProblems: C15 is internally inconsistent. With 2025-26 published tuition of about $39,800 ($41,200 / 1.035) and net tuition per student of $22,950, the 2025 discount rate works out to about 42%, not the stated 47%. The 2026 figure (41%) is consistent.

E5 says the finance committee approved the new schedule on 14 Oct 2025, while C5 says Marrowbridge changed award amounts in the scoring rubric in December. This is plausible as a late hand-off but reads as a minor inconsistency.
Presenting request limits collection to two items, while the task says no limit applies. C1 and C2 together decide the case, so a two-item solver can still reach the key answers.

rulings.explanation: Under the truth convention, the evidence is the initial file (E1–E5) plus the optimal read path (C1, C2). Within that set, H4 rests on two unverified accounts that conflict. E3 says transcripts still showed as 'missing' on 20 Mar after uploads in early January, and the counsellor has the confirmation screens. E4 relays a second-hand claim that every file was complete and blames a status lag. Neither C1 nor C2 covers documents. That fits 'unknown': the claim is live but not established. The 'contradicted' reading depends on C4 and C5, which are off-path, so they should not decide the item. Even if you count them, they do not settle it. C4 leaves 13 of 64 document tickets auto-closed with no resolution, and it contains no file contents. C5 comes from the vendor, an interested party, and only says displays 'can briefly show' pending. A status that stayed wrong for two months is not explained by a brief lag. So H4 cannot be called contradicted, and calling it supported would ignore E4. 'Unknown' is the only defensible answer.

Under the definitions, 'premature' means an action that would be right only if a still-unconfirmed hypothesis were confirmed. A3 does not depend on any unconfirmed hypothesis. E2 establishes that the RD slowdown happened (17 → 31 days median), and E3 shows it damaged counsellor relationships, so a turnaround target is worth having whatever caused the bottleneck. A target sets the outcome and leaves open how to reach it, so the open staffing-vs-module question (R3 association-only) does not make it premature. Admissions may not control the frozen posts, but that does not turn a cheap monitoring target into a commitment that depends on an unconfirmed hypothesis. It is not 'preferred' because C1 shows turnaround did not drive the fall in yield. It is not 'harmful' because it suppresses no information and punishes no one. 'Acceptable' is the only defensible answer.
rulings.fix: No change needed. Optionally, add to the rationale that a target sets an outcome without committing to a particular fix, so the unresolved staffing-vs-module question does not make A3 premature.

rulings.explanation: A4 matches the definition of 'premature' exactly. It would be right if H4 (documents actually lost) were confirmed, but H4 is unknown because the accounts conflict (E3 vs E4). 'Harmful' needs the action to be likely to worsen outcomes, suppress information, punish the wrong party, or disable a protective control. Because H4 is unresolved rather than contradicted, the evidence does not show that the module works. It also does not show that the vendor is the wrong party, or that a rebuild would probably damage the next cycle. 'Wastes resources' is not one of the harm criteria, and nothing in the evidence suggests the rebuild would disable a control. One weakness: the key's rationale says that 'under the remediation clause a needless rebuild costs the university little'. The case evidence never describes the clause's terms, so that sentence relies on an assumption. The answer still stands without it.
rulings.fix: No change to the answer. Delete the unsupported sentence about the remediation clause's cost from the S13 rationale. Alternatively, add one line to the setting or to C5 saying that remediation-clause work is done at the vendor's expense.
